source_title: Climate Change and the New Age of Wildfire in Wine Country
newsletter_intro: Wildfire season is no longer something wine regions can treat as “somewhere else.” This piece looks at what’s happening in France and Spain right now, and why smoke is becoming one more climate reality growers have to plan for. If you love wine, this is one of those big-picture stories worth paying attention to.

slides: Slide 1: Smoke on the horizon isn’t just a weather story. For wine regions, it’s a warning sign.
Slide 2: This summer, wildfires in France and Spain have forced huge evacuations and disrupted life across major wine areas.
Slide 3: Burgundy, Bordeaux, and parts of Spain are all feeling the pressure — even where the vineyards themselves haven’t burned.
Slide 4: Why does smoke matter so much? Because grapes can absorb it, and wines can end up with a smoky, ashy flaw called smoke taint.
Slide 5: We’ve seen this before in California and Australia. The difference now is how widespread and familiar the risk is becoming.
Slide 6: The full post breaks down what this means for wine regions, growers, and the future of terroir. Read it here.

linkedin.post:
Wildfire is no longer a distant climate headline for the wine world. It is becoming a direct operational risk in major regions, from southern Europe to North America and Australia.

In this piece, I look at how recent fires in France and Spain are affecting wine communities, and why smoke exposure matters so much in the vineyard. Grapes are highly sensitive to smoke compounds, and the result can be a flawed vintage long after the flames are gone.

What stands out most is how familiar this pattern has become. California and Australia have already shown us what repeated fire seasons can do to harvests, supply chains, and long-term planning.

For producers, this means more than emergency response. It means rethinking vineyard strategy, smoke monitoring, variety choices, and how we define terroir in a warming climate.

The full post explores what this moment means for growers, regions, and the future of wine.
